title: Two Fixes for the Lock
endLine: Enzymes fit the transition state best, and many change shape.

scenes.tts: Last time, we ended inside an active site, gripping the transition state hardest. But the famous picture of an enzyme is a lock cut for its key. That picture needs two fixes. What are they?
scenes.narration: Last time, we ended inside an active site, gripping the transition state hardest. But the famous picture of an enzyme is a lock cut for its key. That picture needs two fixes. What are they?
scenes.caption: Last time, we ended inside an active site, gripping the transition state hardest. But the famous picture of an enzyme is a lock cut for its key. That picture needs two fixes. What are they?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's world and colour map without a reset, rearranged. TOP STRIP (upper 28% of the frame): the first film's landscape, the same computed curve G(x) = s(x) + H*exp(-(x/1.1)^2) with s(x) = -1.3 - 0.7*tanh(x/1.6), the RED dashed high pass (H = 4.2) and the TEAL lowered pass (H = 1.8); YELLOW dots jiggle in the left valley and a few per second cross the TEAL pass into the right valley; a 'schematic' tag (TEXT, 28) sits at the strip's bottom-right whenever the strip is on screen. MAIN STAGE (below the strip, the subject filling about 60% of the frame height): the first film's TEAL cup-shaped active site, closed snugly on the PURPLE transition-state oval with eight GOLD contact ticks. COLOUR MAP as in the first film: YELLOW substrate, GREEN product, RED the high pass and anything ruled out, TEAL the enzyme and the lowered pass, PURPLE the transition state, GOLD the enzyme's grip. New in this film: ORANGE for Fischer's rigid lock picture, CYAN water, BLUE phosphate, MAGENTA the drug. Labels size 30+, full opacity, at most 5 words, at most 6 things on screen. No molecular structures anywhere: dots, blobs, cups, chips, cartoon outlines. NO fade from black. On 'gripping the transition state hardest' the eight GOLD ticks flash once. On 'famous picture' the cup slides to the left third and an ORANGE rigid lock slides in at centre-right: a flat block with a slot cut in it (cartoon, hard straight edges). A round YELLOW key-dot drops into the slot with a click and fits exactly, no gaps. On 'two fixes' two empty chip outlines appear above the lock, labelled '1' and '2' (TEXT, 34). On 'What are they?' a '?' (40) pops into each chip.
Title 'Two Fixes for the Lock' (TITLE_FONT 54) fades in over the dimmed stage for 2 s, a GOLD rule beneath it. Dots keep crossing the TEAL pass in the top strip. Title out in the last 0.4 s.

scenes.tts: In eighteen ninety four, Emil Fischer explained why an enzyme acts on one sugar and ignores its near-twin. His answer: enzyme and sugar fit like a lock and key.
scenes.narration: In 1894, Emil Fischer explained why an enzyme acts on one sugar and ignores its near-twin. His answer: enzyme and sugar fit like a lock and key.
scenes.caption: In 1894, Emil Fischer explained why an enzyme acts on one sugar and ignores its near-twin. His answer: enzyme and sugar fit like a lock and key.
scenes.visual: The TEAL cup dims to 40% in the left third; the ORANGE lock grows to fill about 60% of the frame height at centre-right. Label 'Fischer, 1894' (ORANGE, 30) above it. On 'one sugar' the round YELLOW dot slides into the slot and seats exactly. On 'near-twin' it slides out and a second YELLOW dot, identical except for one small bump on the opposite side (a mirror-shaped cartoon, not a structure), tries the slot, catches on the rim and bounces away. On 'lock and key' the first dot seats again and a chip 'specificity' (TEXT, 30) settles under the lock. The top strip's dots keep crossing.

scenes.tts: Fix one is about fit. A rigid lock cut for the substrate would hold the substrate most tightly. Enzymes don't. Haldane and Pauling argued that the site fits the transition state best.
scenes.narration: Fix one is about fit. A rigid lock cut for the substrate would hold the substrate most tightly. Enzymes don't. Haldane and Pauling argued that the site fits the transition state best.
scenes.caption: Fix one is about fit. A rigid lock cut for the substrate would hold the substrate most tightly. Enzymes don't. Haldane and Pauling argued that the site fits the transition state best.
scenes.visual: On 'Fix one' chip '1' fills PURPLE with the word 'fit' (30). On 'cut for the substrate' eight GOLD contact ticks light all round the YELLOW dot seated in the ORANGE slot. On 'Enzymes don't' a RED cross stamps over those eight ticks and they fade. On 'Haldane and Pauling' a label 'Haldane, Pauling' (PURPLE, 30) appears; the TEAL cup returns to full brightness at centre-left: a YELLOW dot drops in and sits loosely with only two GOLD ticks, then stretches into the PURPLE oval and the cup closes snugly on it with eight GOLD ticks. On 'fits the transition state best' a label 'best fit: transition state' (PURPLE, 30) settles under the cup.

scenes.tts: Fix two is about shape. Locks don't change shape. In nineteen fifty eight, Daniel Koshland proposed induced fit. His case was hexokinase, which moves a phosphate onto glucose.
scenes.narration: Fix two is about shape. Locks don't change shape. In 1958, Daniel Koshland proposed induced fit. His case was hexokinase, which moves a phosphate onto glucose.
scenes.caption: Fix two is about shape. Locks don't change shape. In 1958, Daniel Koshland proposed induced fit. His case was hexokinase, which moves a phosphate onto glucose.
scenes.visual: On 'Fix two' chip '2' fills TEAL with the word 'shape' (30). On 'Locks don't change shape' YELLOW dots tap the ORANGE lock from three sides; its outline stays perfectly rigid, not one edge moves. The lock then fades out for good, and the 'Haldane, Pauling' and 'best fit' labels go with it. On 'Koshland' a label 'Koshland, 1958' (TEAL, 30) appears. On 'hexokinase' the TEAL cup moves to centre and redraws, larger, as a wide-open cleft with two hinged lips, each lip carrying a small TEAL knob (a catalytic group, cartoon only); label 'hexokinase' (TEAL, 30). A BLUE chip 'phosphate from ATP' (28) sits on the right lip. On 'onto glucose' a YELLOW dot labelled 'glucose' (YELLOW, 30) drifts near the opening. The top strip keeps running.

scenes.tts: Water carries the same O H group as glucose, and water is everywhere. An open site should let water take the phosphate instead. It doesn't. Why not?
scenes.narration: Water carries the same OH group as glucose, and water is everywhere. An open site should let water take the phosphate instead. It doesn't. Why not?
scenes.caption: Water carries the same OH group as glucose, and water is everywhere. An open site should let water take the phosphate instead. It doesn't. Why not?
scenes.visual: On 'Water' a crowd of about fifteen small CYAN dots drifts in all round the open cleft, far outnumbering the single YELLOW glucose; one label 'water' (CYAN, 30). On 'same O H group' a small tag 'OH' (28) appears on the glucose dot and on one water dot. On 'An open site should let water' a CYAN dot slips into the open cleft and a dashed ghost arrow (50% opacity: what should happen) carries the BLUE phosphate toward it. On 'It doesn't' the ghost arrow vanishes and the phosphate stays on the lip. On 'Why not?' a question card slides up in the lower third: 'Why doesn't water take it?' (TEXT, 34).

Thinking pause. The question card stays. Near silence. Gentle motion only: CYAN water dots drift in and out of the open cleft, the YELLOW glucose hovers near the opening, the hinged lips sway slightly, dots keep crossing the TEAL pass in the top strip.

scenes.tts: Because the open site is not ready. Glucose binding closes it, bringing the catalytic groups into line. Water is too small to force that closing. Binding induces the fit. Crystal structures later bore this out for many enzymes.
scenes.narration: Because the open site is not ready. Glucose binding closes it, bringing the catalytic groups into line. Water is too small to force that closing. Binding induces the fit. Crystal structures later bore this out for many enzymes.
scenes.caption: Because the open site is not ready. Glucose binding closes it, bringing the catalytic groups into line. Water is too small to force that closing. Binding induces the fit. Crystal structures later bore this out for many enzymes.
scenes.visual: Card gone. On 'not ready' the CYAN dot inside the cleft drifts out again and the lips stay put. On 'Glucose binding closes it' the YELLOW glucose drops in and both lips swing shut around it; on 'into line' the two TEAL knobs swing into position on either side, and a short GOLD line links knob, BLUE phosphate and glucose in a row. On 'Water is too small' a small inset at the right (about 30% of frame height) replays the open cleft with only a CYAN dot inside: the lips do not move. On 'Binding induces the fit' the inset fades and a label 'induced fit' (TEAL, 30) settles under the closed cleft. On 'many enzymes' a chip 'many enzymes flex' (TEAL, 28) appears beside it.

scenes.tts: Later work added a second route. Many enzymes already shift between open and closed shapes before substrate arrives. The substrate picks the one that fits. That is conformational selection. Real enzymes often mix both.
scenes.narration: Later work added a second route. Many enzymes already shift between open and closed shapes before substrate arrives. The substrate picks the one that fits. That is conformational selection. Real enzymes often mix both.
scenes.caption: Later work added a second route. Many enzymes already shift between open and closed shapes before substrate arrives. The substrate picks the one that fits. That is conformational selection. Real enzymes often mix both.
scenes.visual: Glucose, phosphate and the water crowd fade; the 'many enzymes flex' chip goes. On 'already shift' the empty cleft flips on its own between open and closed, about once every 1.5 s, with nothing bound; label 'open and closed, unbound' (TEAL, 30). On 'picks the one that fits' a YELLOW dot arrives during a closed moment, settles in, and the cleft stays closed. On 'conformational selection' that label (TEAL, 30) replaces the 'open and closed' label. On 'mix both' two short arrows converge on the closed cleft from left and right, labelled 'induced fit' and 'selection' (TEAL, 28), and a chip 'often both' (TEXT, 30) sits between them.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. What an active site fits best, and whether it changes shape, are separate questions. The answers: the transition state, and in many enzymes, yes.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. What an active site fits best, and whether it changes shape, are separate questions. The answers: the transition state, and in many enzymes, yes.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. What an active site fits best, and whether it changes shape, are separate questions. The answers: the transition state, and in many enzymes, yes.
scenes.visual: Reset to the central picture: top strip running, the TEAL cup at centre closed snugly on the PURPLE oval with eight GOLD ticks. On 'Here is the one idea' everything else fades. On 'fits best' a chip 'fits best?' (TEXT, 30) appears at upper left of the stage; on 'changes shape' a chip 'changes shape?' (TEXT, 30) appears at upper right. On 'separate questions' a vertical WHITE divider grows down between the two chips, splitting the stage. On 'the transition state' the left chip fills PURPLE and reads 'transition state', and the PURPLE oval in the cup glows. On 'in many enzymes, yes' the right chip fills TEAL and reads 'many enzymes: yes', and the cup's lips open and close once.

scenes.tts: The first answer reaches medicine. Picture a molecule that binds the site more tightly than the substrate does. If the enzyme cannot turn it over, it can shut the enzyme down. Drugs shaped like a transition state exploit this.
scenes.narration: The first answer reaches medicine. Picture a molecule that binds the site more tightly than the substrate does. If the enzyme cannot turn it over, it can shut the enzyme down. Drugs shaped like a transition state exploit this.
scenes.caption: The first answer reaches medicine. Picture a molecule that binds the site more tightly than the substrate does. If the enzyme cannot turn it over, it can shut the enzyme down. Drugs shaped like a transition state exploit this.
scenes.visual: The two answer chips shrink into the top corners of the stage; the divider fades; the cup reopens and the PURPLE oval leaves. On 'Picture a molecule' a MAGENTA blob slides into the open cup and the lips close on it; GOLD ticks light all round it, more than the two a YELLOW substrate gets. On 'cannot turn it over' a YELLOW substrate dot bumps the occupied cup and bounces off; up in the top strip the stream of dots over the TEAL pass thins to nothing and the valley dots just jiggle. On 'shaped like a transition state' the MAGENTA blob's outline stretches into the same stretched-oval silhouette as the PURPLE transition state, and a label 'transition-state-shaped drug' (MAGENTA, 30) appears.

scenes.tts: Statins get there another way. They block H M G co A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Part of each statin mimics the H M G part of the substrate and fills its pocket.
scenes.narration: Statins get there another way. They block HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Part of each statin mimics the HMG part of the substrate and fills its pocket.
scenes.caption: Statins get there another way. They block HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Part of each statin mimics the HMG part of the substrate and fills its pocket.
scenes.visual: The top strip and the corner chips fade out (they return in s13). The TEAL cup reopens empty and gets the label 'HMG-CoA reductase' (TEAL, 30). Along the bottom of the frame a schematic pathway arrow draws from left to right: 'HMG-CoA' at the start, three plain step ticks, 'cholesterol' at the end (TEXT, 28); YELLOW dots flow along it through the cup. On 'Statins' the MAGENTA blob returns redrawn as a two-part shape: one end is a copy of the YELLOW substrate's end outline in MAGENTA, label 'HMG-like part' (MAGENTA, 28), the other end a longer MAGENTA tail. Not a structure: two simple outlines joined. On 'fills its pocket' the HMG-like end slides into the cup's pocket and seats.

scenes.tts: Extra contacts nearby let it bind far more tightly than the substrate. Sitting in the active site and keeping the substrate out, it is a competitive inhibitor. Slowing the pathway makes the liver pull more L D L cholesterol from the blood.
scenes.narration: Extra contacts nearby let it bind far more tightly than the substrate. Sitting in the active site and keeping the substrate out, it is a competitive inhibitor. Slowing the pathway makes the liver pull more LDL cholesterol from the blood.
scenes.caption: Extra contacts nearby let it bind far more tightly than the substrate. Sitting in the active site and keeping the substrate out, it is a competitive inhibitor. Slowing the pathway makes the liver pull more LDL cholesterol from the blood.
scenes.visual: On 'Extra contacts nearby' the MAGENTA tail lies along the cup's rim and a row of extra GOLD ticks lights along it (schematic, no count); label 'far tighter than substrate' (MAGENTA, 30). On 'keeping the substrate out' a YELLOW HMG-CoA dot bumps the occupied pocket and stays outside; the label changes to 'competitive inhibitor' (MAGENTA, 30). On 'Slowing the pathway' the YELLOW flow along the pathway arrow slows to a trickle. On 'the liver' the cup slides left and a large pale outline of a liver cell, labelled 'liver cell' (TEXT, 30), fills the right half, a RED band labelled 'blood' (RED, 28) beside it; on 'pull more L D L' WHITE-ringed dots labelled 'LDL' (28) move from the blood band into the liver cell, faster than before. Direction only, no amounts.

scenes.tts: So ask two things of any active site. What is it built to fit? The fleeting top of the climb. Does it move? Locks never do. Many enzymes do.
scenes.narration: So ask two things of any active site. What is it built to fit? The fleeting top of the climb. Does it move? Locks never do. Many enzymes do.
scenes.caption: So ask two things of any active site. What is it built to fit? The fleeting top of the climb. Does it move? Locks never do. Many enzymes do.
scenes.visual: The liver cell, pathway and statin fade. Restore the central picture: top strip running, TEAL cup at centre closed snugly on the PURPLE oval with eight GOLD ticks, the two answer chips back at upper left ('transition state', PURPLE) and upper right ('many enzymes: yes', TEAL). On 'built to fit' the PURPLE oval glows; on 'top of the climb' a thin PURPLE line rises from the oval to the top of the TEAL pass in the strip, and the transition-state point there glows PURPLE. On 'Does it move?' the cup's lips open and close once. On 'Locks never do' a faint ORANGE ghost of Fischer's rigid lock appears beside the cup, perfectly still, then fades. On 'Many enzymes do' the cup closes again on the oval and dots stream over the TEAL pass.

End card over the living world at 20% opacity: dots still crossing the TEAL pass in the strip, the TEAL cup breathing open and closed around the PURPLE oval. LINE (TITLE_FONT 40), centred: 'Enzymes fit the transition state best, and many change shape.'
